title: Don’t Be Fooled by Victories—The USMNT Still Has Several Questions Left to Answer
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Sophia VeselyOct 8, 2026Mauricio Pochettino still has many tactical problems to solve. / Taylor Banner/USSF/Getty ImagesThe U.S. men’s national team looks fantastic. This fact cannot be denied, and the team has four-straight wins to back it up.
Nonetheless, two things can be true. The USMNT can be categorically perfect post-2026 World Cup, yet still harbor several imperfections.

Manager Mauricio Pochettino is undoubtedly proud of the way the Stars and Stripes dominated in their first regrouping since the summer’s tournament; however, he is left with just as many questions as when the team was unexpectedly thrashed by Belgium in the round of 16.

There are several unknowns that relate to individual American players, such as the future status of once-leader Christian Pulisic or former stalwart Tim Weah. There are also several broader, team-centered and positional problems Pochettino must puzzle through.
Here are three big questions Pochettino still has left to answer. Thankfully, he has four years to do so.

Matt Freese could be on his way out. / Mark Thorstenson/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesPochettino has dreams of turning the USMNT into one of the “most powerful” international teams in global soccer, one that can repeatedly contend for regional trophies and advance deep into World Cup competition.

That is a dream he will never achieve without an elite goalkeeper. Not only is a stellar shot-stopper the difference between beating good teams and great teams, it also sets the entire mood of a team’s play. Having unwavering confidence in one’s last line of defense enables a squad to be carefree enough to reach a flow state and take chances.

The Stars and Stripes have not had a world-class goalkeeper of longevity on their roster in nearly 10 years, back when Tim Howard retired in 2017. The Premier League star and two-time World Cup starter (2010, 2014) had 42 clean sheets in 121 total caps for the national team, amounting to nearly 35% of his appearances.

Meanwhile, the 2026 World Cup starting goalkeeper, Matt Freese, has five clean sheets in 19 total caps (26%), an underperformance compared to Howard’s statistics and a sincere lack of experience to be handed the keys to the net at soccer’s most prestigious affair. The reality that Freese was in over his head manifested most obviously in the round of 16 loss, when he whiffed a clearance to gift Belgium its third goal of the night, the nail in the coffin for a runaway victory.

Pochettino has had wavering faith in Freese, and even called him up for the fall. Freese played just 45 minutes against Peru, though, in a rather uneventful outing that saw him make a single save.

The rest of the goalkeeping ranks aren’t promising either. World Cup third-stringer Chris Brady and newcomers Brian Schwake and Diego Kochen all underwhelmed. To be fair, none of them were heavily tested. Nevertheless, there were not even glimpses of world-class play. At best, they were solid, but that’s not enough to turn Pochettino’s team into a global superpower.
Chris Richards is the heartbeat of the backline. / David Berding/USSF/Getty ImagesThank goodness for Chris Richards.

The seasoned veteran has been a constant in the center of the backline since early 2025, impressing with his distribution skills of unfathomable accuracy, his aerial dominance, his one-on-one defending and, most importantly, his poise. He sets a tone of cool confidence across the entire defense that can then instigate dangerous attacking motions.

He can’t do it alone, though. With the recent international retirement of 39-year-old Tim Ream, the need for a suitable partner has never been clearer, yet no obvious contender has presented himself thus far.

There’s Mark McKenzie and Auston Trusty, both of whom are fringe players. Trusty did partner well with Richards when called upon this fall, though. There is also Miles Robinson; however, the more minutes he accrues on the international stage, the more he seems incorrect for the job.

Pochettino will certainly be holding out hope for Neil Pierre, who has held down the Philadelphia Union’s backline since their MLS resurgence this summer. Except the 6'7" teenager struggled in his debut camp this fall, proving he still has a lot of work to do before he can even begin to enter the starting lineup conversation. He made one start in the win against Chile and continuously gave the ball away, resulting in unnecessary counter attacks for the South Americans. Pochettino ultimately couldn’t trust him again, granting him zero minutes against Mexico and just 16 against Canada.

The USMNT is a tight-knit group. / Maja Hitij/FIFA/Getty ImagesThe gap between the USMNT’s most successful moments at the World Cup this summer and the catastrophe that ensued against Belgium can be chiefly attested to one factor: the team’s identity.

At its peak, the USMNT played with a rugged grit that manifested into a high-press, aggressive attacking strategy. From the opening whistle, the Americans jumped down their opponents’ throats and didn’t give them any other choice but sit back and be dictated by their rhythm of play. In all three group stage matches, they found the back of the net within the first 11 minutes.
